issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette:
Kiet Nguyen was twenty-two years old when he found himself on the ground in the middle of a public market, debris raining down around him, his ears ringing with a sound he would later learn was the detonation of a suicide vest. He had been buying vegetables for his mother when the world split open. In the aftermath, he did not stay to help the wounded. He did not check on the elderly woman who had been standing beside him, whose groceries had scattered across the pavement. He got up and he ran. He ran until his legs gave out, and then he sat in an alley and shook until someone found him. In the months and years that followed, that moment of running became the axis around which everything else seemed to turn.

He did not think of it that way at first. In the beginning, he simply tried not to think about it at all. He threw himself into his work at the bank with an intensity that surprised his manager. He volunteered for the earliest shifts, the latest closing duties, the inventory tasks no one else wanted. If he was busy, he discovered, he could keep the images at bay. If he was exhausted, he could fall into bed without the slow spiral of replaying every detail. He began to work six days a week, then seven. His wife at the time — a kind woman he had married young, before the bombing — began to complain that he was never home, and when he was home, he was not really there. He would sit on the couch staring at the television without seeing it, his jaw tight, his hands clenched. She would touch his shoulder and he would flinch. She would ask what was wrong and he would say nothing, because he did not have the words, and because saying it out loud felt like opening a door he had spent every waking hour trying to keep shut.

The divorce came two years later. He signed the papers without much of a fight. By then he had already accepted that he was not someone who could be close to another person. Intimacy required a kind of openness that felt dangerous, like standing in an open field with no cover. He had learned that safety meant keeping people at a distance, keeping himself guarded, keeping his thoughts locked away where no one could see them.

At work, his colleagues noticed the change. Kiet had once been patient and easygoing; now he snapped at customers who took too long at his window, muttered under his breath when someone asked a question he found obvious, slammed his drawer shut when a transaction frustrated him. Twice, a supervisor had pulled him aside to ask if everything was alright. Both times, Kiet nodded and said he was fine. He was not fine. He woke three or four times a night, sitting bolt upright in the dark, his heart pounding, scanning the corners of his bedroom for threats that were not there. He would get up and check the locks on his apartment door, then check them again, then slide a chair under the handle before he could get back to sleep. Walking to and from the bank, he found himself glancing over his shoulder constantly, scanning faces in the crowd, noting exits, watching for anyone who might be moving too quickly or too purposefully. He could not stop. He did not even realize he was doing it most of the time — the scanning had become as automatic as breathing.

What he did realize, with a growing sense of horror, was that he no longer recognized himself. He had been raised to believe that a good person helped others, that a man protected those around him, that courage meant rising to the moment. And when his moment had come, he had run. He had left people behind. He had saved himself and nothing else. This thought had taken root in him like a splinter that could not be removed. He was not the person he had thought he was. He could not rely on himself to do the right thing when it mattered. The things that had once defined him — his sense of duty, his reliability, his belief that he was fundamentally good — had been stripped away in those few seconds after the explosion, and he had not found a way to get them back.

He came to therapy because his manager gave him an ultimatum after he screamed at a customer who had accidentally set off the bank's alarm. The sound had sent him into a state he could not control. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, already scanning the exits, already calculating how long it would take to get to the door. What he wanted, more than anything, was to stop feeling like a stranger in his own body. But what he feared was that the person he had become during those seconds in the market was not a stranger at all. It was who he really was. And he was not sure if therapy could change that.
